subject: Runtime bifurcation & proxy-adapter review for private VPC deployment
messages:
From: Samir Patel <samir@atlascloud.com>
To: Grace O'Connor <grace_oconnor@redwood.ai>
Cc: Jonas Weber <jonas_weber@redwood.ai>
Date: Mon, 8 Mar 2027 09:12:00 -0700
Subject: Runtime bifurcation & proxy-adapter proposal for our on‑prem clusters

Hi Grace (+Jonas),

Thanks again for the call today. As discussed, AtlasCloud needs a reference approach so our infra team can decide whether to host the control plane in a shared Redwood-managed VPC while keeping inference nodes air-gapped in customer-owned colo racks. The two main asks from our side:

- A clear diagram showing control-plane-to-data-plane connectivity when the data plane is behind a NAT / egress-only proxy.
- A fallback pattern for KV cache access when direct low-latency links are unavailable (we proposed a sidecar proxy that can do prefix-level cache mirroring).

I've attached a preliminary sketch and a short ops checklist. Can you confirm whether Redwood supports: (1) a control-plane mesh with per-tenant L4 host bridges, and (2) an opt-in sidecar adapter that translates the runtime K/V cache calls to an in-cluster proxy?

Attachment: runtime-bifurcation-diagram-v3.png (image/png)
Attachment: ops-integration-checklist.xlsx (application/vnd.openxmlformats-officedocument.spreadsheetml.sheet)

Next steps we'd like: a short doc (2–3 pages) with the recommended patterns plus any constraints for compliance (no LAN egress, only outbound TLS to Redwood endpoints).

Cheers,
Samir
Senior Product Ops, AtlasCloud
From: Grace O'Connor <grace_oconnor@redwood.ai>
To: Samir Patel <samir@atlascloud.com>
Cc: Jonas Weber <jonas_weber@redwood.ai>, Mina Haddad <mina_haddad@redwood.ai>
Date: Mon, 8 Mar 2027 11:05:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Runtime bifurcation & proxy-adapter proposal for our on‑prem clusters

Samir — thanks for the clear recap and attachments. Short answer: yes, we can support the pattern but with a few caveats. High-level notes below; Mina and Jonas, please weigh in on operational constraints.

1) Control-plane meshing: Redwood can run a federated control plane where the central control plane speaks to on‑prem agents over outbound TLS. We recommend a single egress endpoint per colo for observability simplicity (certificate pinning + mTLS from agent).

2) Host-bridge vs tunnel: For tenants that cannot accept inbound, we use an outbound mesh connector (think persistent TLS tunnel) rather than inbound bridges. That preserves customer policy (no inbound).

3) KV cache sidecar: feasible. Two modes:
   - Local sidecar mirror: keeps hot prefixes on the tenant's data plane. Requires eventual consistency and eviction policies.
   - Proxy-to-cloud: sidecar forwards cache-miss traffic outbound to Redwood cache tier with batching. Better for consistency but adds egress latency.

Constraints: billing/monitoring hooks for sidecars, retention of logs for SOC2 requests (customer must agree to outbound observability endpoints), and a rollback plan if the sidecar saturates NICs.

I'll draft the 2–3 page pattern doc and a simple diagram. Question for AtlasCloud: can your colo allow an outbound static IP or do we need dynamic egress that requires mutual TLS certificate discovery?

— Grace
Director, Private Deployments | Redwood Inference

On Tue, Mar 9, 2027 at 11:05 AM Grace O'Connor <grace_oconnor@redwood.ai> wrote:
> Samir — thanks for the clear recap and attachments. Short answer: yes, we can support the pattern but with a few caveats.
> 
> Question for AtlasCloud: can your colo allow an outbound static IP or do we need dynamic egress that requires mutual TLS certificate discovery?

Hi Grace — we have two colo classes. The modern racks allow a static egress NAT IP per tenant; older sites use carrier NAT and provide only dynamic egress. For the pilot (two customers) we can guarantee static egress. For broader rollout, we'll need a TLS-based discovery flow.

Also included Alex (ops lead) — Alex, would you review the diagram and confirm whether the sidecar mirror approach will be limited by our current NVMe caching limits (we plan 2TB per rack).

Thanks,
Samir
From: Grace O'Connor <grace_oconnor@redwood.ai>
To: Jonas Weber <jonas_weber@redwood.ai>, Mina Haddad <mina_haddad@redwood.ai>, Alex Chen <alex.chen@customerco.com>
Date: Thu, 11 Mar 2027 15:42:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Runtime bifurcation & proxy-adapter proposal for our on‑prem clusters

Alex / team — quick readout from Redwood side after internal sync. Key decisions and ops actions: 

- Pilot mode (static egress): support both sidecar-mirror and proxy-to-cloud. Default = proxy-to-cloud for first 90 days to avoid local eviction surprises.
- Discovery: implement a lightweight mTLS enrollment API. If static egress is present, we bind certificate to the IP for simplified routing.
- Observability: sidecar will emit a condensed telemetry stream (token hashed) back to Redwood for cache hit-rate and quota accounting. Customer must opt-in for log retention beyond 30 days.
- Fail-open behavior: sidecar must fail into a local degraded inference mode (requests served with reduced KV cache guarantees) rather than silent drops.

Action items (owners):
- Jonas: define enrollment API + cert rotation schedule (due 2027-03-18).
- Mina: draft sidecar resource limits and gating (NIC, memory, eviction policy) (due 2027-03-16).
- Grace: produce 2-page pattern doc and a simplified diagram we can hand to AtlasCloud by 2027-03-12.

Alex — can you confirm NVMe sizing and whether 2TB per rack is fixed for the pilot? If not, we'll assume the proxy-to-cloud default.

Thanks all — attaching the revised diagram with the gateway fallback highlighted.

Attachment: runtime-bifurcation-diagram-v3.png (revised callouts)

— Grace
Director, Private Deployments | Redwood Inference
